n: Watching Jesus pray makes the disciples want to learn how. Rabbis often gave their followers a characteristic prayer, as John the Baptist had done, so one disciple asks Jesus for His.
Jesus begins with God: He is our Father, His name is holy, and we long for His kingdom and will to prevail on earth as in heaven. Prayer starts by aligning our desires with His.
We ask for what we need today — and then again tomorrow. Like manna in the wilderness, daily dependence keeps us close to God.
We seek forgiveness while forgiving others, and we plead for protection from trial and evil. Receiving mercy and extending it go together.

f.g: Owing us — anyone who has wronged us.
JST Matthew 6:14 reads “suffer us not to be led into temptation.”

n: Jesus tells a story: imagine going to a friend’s house at midnight to borrow three loaves of bread.

f.g: Small flat loaves — enough for a meal for one guest.

n: An unexpected traveler has arrived, and in that culture failing to feed a guest was shameful. The need is real and urgent.
The friend inside complains: the door is barred and the whole family is asleep in one room. Getting up would wake everyone.

f.g: Village doors were secured with a heavy bar at night.

n: Even if friendship isn’t enough, the persistent asking will get him out of bed. If a reluctant neighbor responds to persistence, how much more will a loving God respond?
Jesus gives three invitations with three promises: ask and receive, seek and find, knock and the door opens. These words echo throughout scripture and helped launch the Restoration.

f.w: Ask, and it shall be given you

n: The promise is universal: everyone who asks receives. God’s answers may differ from what we expect, but He always hears and responds.
No loving father would hand his hungry son a stone that looks like bread, or a snake instead of a fish.
Nor would he give a scorpion — perhaps a curled-up one that looks like an egg. Earthly parents don’t trick their children.

f.g: Some scorpions in the region are pale and, when curled, could resemble an egg.

n: If imperfect human parents give good gifts, our Heavenly Father will surely give His greatest gift — the Holy Ghost — to those who ask. Luke emphasizes the Spirit throughout his Gospel and Acts.

f.w: give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him

n: Jesus casts out a spirit that had made a man unable to speak. When it leaves, the man talks, and the crowd is amazed.
Some critics can’t deny the miracle, so they attack its source, claiming Jesus works by the power of the prince of devils.

f.g: Possibly “lord of the flies” or “lord of the dwelling,” a name for Satan.

n: Others test Him by demanding a sign from heaven — as if the miracle just performed weren’t enough.
Jesus, knowing their thoughts, answers with common sense: any kingdom or household fighting itself will fall apart.
If Satan were casting out his own servants, he’d be destroying his own kingdom. Their accusation makes no sense.
Some Jewish exorcists also cast out spirits. If the critics accept those, their own followers will testify against the double standard.
If Jesus is acting by God’s power, then God’s kingdom has arrived among them. “The finger of God” recalls the miracles in Egypt that even Pharaoh’s magicians recognized.
Picture a strong, armed man guarding his house; his possessions seem safe. Satan is that strong man, holding people captive.
But someone stronger comes, defeats him, strips his armor, and divides the plunder. Christ is the Stronger One who frees Satan’s captives.
There is no neutral ground. Those not actively gathering with Christ are, in effect, scattering.

f.w: He that is not with me is against me

n: A spirit cast out wanders through barren places looking for rest, finds none, and decides to return to the person it left.

f.g: Desert regions, thought to be haunts of evil spirits.

n: It finds the house cleaned and decorated — but empty. Removing evil isn’t enough; the heart must be filled with something good.
It brings seven worse spirits, and the person ends up worse off than before. Reformation without filling the life with God leaves us vulnerable.

f.w: the last state of that man is worse than the first

n: A woman in the crowd calls out a blessing on Jesus’ mother — a typical way of praising a remarkable son.
Jesus doesn’t deny His mother’s blessedness, but points to something even greater and available to everyone: hearing God’s word and keeping it.

f.w: hear the word of God, and keep it

n: As crowds grow, Jesus rebukes the demand for signs. The only sign they’ll receive is the sign of Jonah.

f.g: Greek form of the name Jonah.

n: Jonah himself — a prophet who came back as if from death — was a sign to Nineveh. Jesus, rising from the dead, will be the sign to His generation.

f.g: People of Nineveh, capital of Assyria.

n: The Queen of Sheba traveled a great distance to hear Solomon’s wisdom. Someone far greater than Solomon is here, yet many will not cross the street to hear Him.

f.g: The Queen of Sheba, probably from southern Arabia.

n: Nineveh repented at Jonah’s brief message. These pagans will stand as witnesses against a generation that ignored a far greater prophet.

f.w: a greater than Jonas is here

n: Light is meant to be displayed, not hidden under a basket. Jesus is that light, openly offered to all.

f.g: A basket or container for measuring grain.

n: The eye is like a window letting light into the body. A “single” eye — focused wholly on God — fills the whole person with light; a corrupt eye lets in darkness.
Be careful that what you think is light inside you isn’t actually darkness. Self-deception is a real danger.
When a person is completely filled with light, with no dark corners, they shine as brightly as a lamp. This is the goal of discipleship.
A Pharisee invites Jesus to a meal, and He accepts. Luke often shows Jesus eating with all kinds of people, including His critics.

f.g: Reclined at the table for a meal.

n: The host is shocked that Jesus skips the ceremonial hand-washing — not a hygiene rule but a religious tradition added to the law.

f.g: Ritual washing required by Pharisaic tradition, not by the law of Moses.

n: Jesus uses dishes as a metaphor: the Pharisees scrub the outside of cups but leave the inside filthy — clean in appearance, greedy and wicked within.
God made both the outside and the inside of a person. How foolish to care only for appearances when He sees the heart.

f.g: Senseless ones — a sharp but not hateful rebuke.

n: Instead, give generously from the heart. Inner generosity cleanses far more than outward washing.
They carefully tithe even tiny garden herbs, but neglect justice and love for God. Jesus doesn’t dismiss tithing — He says do both, but don’t lose the weightier matters.

f.g: A bitter herb used for seasoning and medicine.

n: They crave the best seats and public honor. Their religion has become a stage for status.

f.g: The front seats facing the congregation, reserved for honored people.

n: Touching a grave made a Jew ritually unclean. The hypocrites are like unmarked graves — people are defiled by them without even knowing it.

f.g: Unmarked graves; tombs were usually whitewashed so people could avoid them.

n: A legal scholar protests that Jesus is insulting them too.
Jesus answers: yes, you too. Experts pile heavy rules on people but won’t lift a finger to help them carry the load.
They honor dead prophets by building monuments, while their ancestors killed those prophets — and they’re about to do the same to the living ones.
By building the tombs, they are finishing what their fathers began — the fathers killed, the sons bury. They are approving their ancestors’ deeds.
God’s wisdom foresaw that He would send prophets and apostles, and that some would be killed and persecuted.

f.g: Perhaps referring to God speaking in His wisdom; Matthew presents these as Jesus’ own words.

n: The guilt of all the righteous blood shed throughout history will be held against this generation, which is rejecting the greatest Prophet of all.
From Abel, the first murder in Genesis, to Zechariah, the last in the Hebrew Bible’s order of books (2 Chronicles) — the whole span of scripture’s martyrs.
These experts hold the key to understanding scripture but neither enter themselves nor let others in. The JST says the key they took away was “the fulness of the scriptures.”

f.g: JST Luke 11:53: “the key of knowledge, the fulness of the scriptures.”

n: Furious, the scribes and Pharisees start grilling Jesus aggressively, firing questions to provoke Him.
They lie in wait, hoping to trap Him into saying something they could use against Him. The opposition that leads to the cross is growing.
